facts.claim: Ranks companies by similarity to your best customers, starting from a plain-English description of your ideal customer or from your existing customers.
Lets you narrow results with phrases from company homepages (the page's example: 'rooftop unit service').
Also sells contact data with verified emails. This skill does not cover contact data.
Pricing shown on the page: a one-time $5 credit with no card, pay-as-you-go at $5 per 1,000 records, subscriptions from $99 to $1,599 a month.
Company Lookalike needs a seed domain up front. Industry, size, technologies and location filters are optional.
In Clay, the Ocean.io lookalike source takes up to 10 domains as seed companies. That limit is Clay's integration, not necessarily Ocean.io's own.
Apollo says you can search its contact database with 65+ filters, including firmographic and technographic filters, before spending credits.
Its company data says every company in TheirStack is discovered through job postings.
Job search filters by title, technology, salary, location and 20+ other attributes, and can be combined with company filters.
Technology usage is inferred from job postings, with confidence scoring.
Pricing page showed 1,000 company credits for $109 ($0.109 per credit).
Extracts names, addresses, websites, phone numbers, ratings, review counts, categories and opening hours from Google Maps.
Priced pay per event. Contact-detail scraping is a separate paid add-on. Check the page for current prices.
Google Maps shows no more than 120 places per area. A scraper listing on Apify says it gets past that limit.

The Apify Store has several community-built actors that search public LinkedIn posts by keyword. Listed prices ranged from $1.50 to $5 per 1,000 posts. At least one listing was marked 'under maintenance'. Check who maintains the actor and when it was last updated.

LinkedIn says third-party software that scrapes or automates activity on LinkedIn, including crawlers, bots and browser extensions, violates its User Agreement (Section 8.2), and accounts using it risk being restricted or shut down.

Article 9(1) prohibits processing personal data that reveals racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs or trade union membership, and genetic, biometric, health, sex-life or sexual-orientation data, unless an Article 9(2) exception applies.

The UK ICO says information scraped from blogs, social media and forum discussions may contain personal data that individuals placed there, and scraping needs a valid lawful basis. That page is about AI training data, so read it as a signal, not as a ruling on lead lists.
